scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Let me know if you’d like help with specific messages or designs!

prediction.raw: This is a **complex interpersonal dynamic**, and whether you acted "right" or "wrong" depends on **balance, communication, and fairness**—not just your feelings or his complaints. Here’s a breakdown of the key issues and why your decision leans toward **AITA (but with nuance)**: --- ### **Why You’re Not *Completely* Wrong (0.8/1)** 1. **Your Effort Justifies Boundaries** - You’ve invested **time, skill, and shared resources** (budget, ingredients) into cooking for the group. His behavior **undermines that effort** by treating your meals like fast food, which is **disrespectful** to your labor. - Your cooking isn’t "perfect," but it’s **consistent, intentional, and valued by others**—that’s a valid reason to set limits. 2. **You Tried Communication First** - You offered **solutions** (making his favorite meals, asking him to try food first) before cutting off his contribution. This shows you weren’t being unreasonable upfront. 3. **His Complaints Are Hypocritical** - He’s **not cooking at all** (eating out/pre-made meals) but complains about his **expenses increasing** because he’s no longer getting free meals. This is **self-serving**—he’s not contributing to the shared effort, yet expects to benefit from it. 4. **Your Other Roommates Support You** - The baking roommate’s agreement gives you **moral support**, while the neutral roommate’s indifference suggests he doesn’t care either way. This reduces the "group pressure" to keep cooking for him. --- ### **Why You’re *Mostly* Wrong (0.2/1)** 1. **You Didn’t Give Him a Clear Alternative** - You told him **"no more fresh ingredients"** but didn’t propose a **fair replacement**. Options could’ve been: - **"I’ll stop cooking for you unless you agree to try food first."** - **"If you don’t want to eat my meals, you can contribute to the shared budget for ingredients *or* cook for yourself."** - **"I’ll make you a separate, condiment-free portion if you promise not to add sauces."** - Instead, you **punished him without solutions**, leaving him with no way to "earn" meals back. 2. **His Behavior Isn’t *Entirely* Your Problem** - While his condiment habit is **rude**, it’s also a **personal preference** (some people genuinely dislike plain food). You could’ve: - **Made condiments available** (e.g., a shared small jar of hot sauce) so he could add them *after* tasting. - **Asked him to eat separately** if he couldn’t respect your cooking. - **Accepted that not everyone will appreciate your meals**—it’s okay if he doesn’t. 3. **You’re Overgeneralizing "Fast Food" Comparison** - You said his behavior is like **"treating my food like fast food"**—but **fast food is cheap and convenient**, while your meals are **shared, intentional, and budgeted**. The comparison is unfair. His issue isn’t the food itself but **his inability to adapt**. 4. **The Shared Budget Was a Two-Way Street** - You’ve **paid for ingredients more than he has**, but you also **accepted non-food payment** (booze, chores, favors). This creates an **imbalance**—if he’s not contributing equally, he shouldn’t expect equal benefits. --- ### **The Verdict: 0.8/1 (Mostly Right, But Could’ve Handled Better)** You **had every right to stop cooking for him** after repeated requests went unheeded, but your **execution lacked fairness**. Here’s how to **fix it** (if you want to reconcile): #### **If You Want to Keep the Boundary:** - **Firmly state:** *"I’m done cooking for you unless you agree to try food first. If you still don’t, you’ll need to contribute to the shared budget or cook for yourself."* - **Document your contributions** (e.g., "I’ve paid for X meals this month; you’ve paid for 0"). This makes it **less about emotion and more about fairness**. #### **If You Want to Reopen the Dialogue:** - **Ask him:** *"What would make you respect my cooking more? Would you be willing to try food first, or would you prefer to cook for yourself?"* - **Offer a compromise:** *"I’ll make you a condiment-free plate if you promise not to add sauces."* #### **If You’re Done:** - **No apology needed.** If he can’t respect your effort, he’s not worth accommodating. Your other roommates’ support validates your stance. --- ### **Key Takeaway** You’re **not being petty**—you’re **protecting your labor and boundaries**. But **punishment without solutions** makes you look unreasonable. Next time, **lead with fairness** (clear rules + alternatives) before cutting off contributions. **Final Score: 0.8/1** (You’re right to stand your ground, but could’ve handled it more diplomatically.)
